content:
在此订阅：Apple 播客 | Spotify |除了 Nvidia 与黄仁勋丑闻的淫秽细节之外，还有一个关于国家安全和推动人工智能繁荣的先进芯片的故事。但这些芯片到底是什么？它们为何如此重要？本·布坎南 (Ben Buchanan) 是拜登总统的人工智能顾问之一，他在与黄这样的人交谈时帮助制定了美国的一些芯片控制政策。在本期《银河大脑》中，他详细分析了这些芯片为何如此有价值，以及它们为何对中美关系和人工智能的未来产生如此大的影响。以下是该集的文字记录： Ben Buchanan：我们与 Jensen 和 Nvidia 进行了很多对话。他们谈论的是技术，而不是间谍或性或类似的东西。所以这是它的一个新维度。但从技术角度来看，这实际上与我们在拜登政府中的担忧非常一致。 [音乐]查理·沃泽尔：我们从英伟达-黄仁勋丑闻中走得越远，就越清楚地看到，尽管有所有淫秽的细节，但这个故事的内涵远比表面上看到的要多得多。是的，这是一起所谓的中国间谍性丑闻。这是科技巨头的陨落。这是一个巨大的硅谷宫廷阴谋故事。但随着时间的推移，这个故事的中心似乎是在华盛顿特区。英伟达与黄仁勋事件本质上是一场地缘政治惊悚片。
这是中美之间关于先进人工智能芯片和人工智能竞赛的冷战引发的一系列连锁事件。因此，要真正理解为什么黄仁勋必须辞职，为什么他被传唤到国会作证，为什么美国证券交易委员会据报道对英伟达发起调查，你必须了解美国是如何陷入与中国的人工智能竞赛中的，以及英伟达的芯片如何推动人工智能的繁荣。你必须了解导致英伟达销售的芯片受到出口限制的政策，以及英伟达和黄爱丽据称利用的复杂漏洞将芯片带入中国。今天我的客人：他不仅理解这个故事的每一个元素，而且还理解这个故事的每一个细节。他帮助塑造它。本·布坎南 (Ben Buchanan) 是拜登政府期间的前白宫人工智能特别顾问。布坎南帮助设计了针对中国的芯片出口管制措施，黄仁勋和英伟达对此进行了游说反对。他与坦图姆·柯林斯 (Tantum Collins) 共同撰写了这本新书《痛苦的斗争：超级智能、超级大国和世界的命运》。他参与了许多事件，导致了我们现在的处境。今天，他将帮助我们这些凡人真正了解中国、芯片、黄仁勋、人工智能竞赛到底发生了什么，以及最重要的是，为什么这一切都很重要。他现在加入我。我是查理·沃泽尔，这是银河大脑。 [音乐] 沃泽尔：本·布坎南，欢迎来到银河大脑。本·布坎南：谢谢你邀请我。
沃泽尔：所以我希望在这次采访中我们可以提出一些非常基本的问题，这将有助于更深入地了解中美竞争、实验室；发生了什么事。但首先我想问一下黄仁勋的情况。您是否根据我们现在所知的情况重新审视了您与他或他的公司的互动？比如，现在回想起来，是否有一些事情看起来像是脆弱的迹象？考虑到您与整个故事的关系，您如何看待这个新闻时刻？布坎南：就背景而言，我是白宫特别顾问

【原文 English Original】
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Beyond the salacious details of the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal is a story about national security and the advanced chips powering the AI boom. But what exactly are these chips, and why do they matter? Ben Buchanan was one of President Biden’s AI advisers and helped write some of the U.S. policies on chip controls, in conversation with people like Huang. In this episode of Galaxy Brain , he breaks down what makes those chips so valuable and why they have such implications for the U.S.-Chinese relationship and the future of AI. The following is a transcript of the episode: Ben Buchanan: We had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. [ Music ] Charlie Warzel: The further we get out from the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal, the more it seems clear that, despite all the salacious details, there’s a lot more to this story than meets the eye. It’s an alleged Chinese-spy sex scandal, yes. It’s the fall of a tech giant. It’s this huge, Silicon Valley palace-intrigue story. But as time goes by, it seems that the epicenter of this story is in Washington, D.C. The Nvidia–Jensen Huang affair is, at heart, a geopolitical thriller. It is a series of cascading events that’s been set in motion by a cold war between China and the United States over advanced AI chips and the AI race. And so to really understand why Huang had to resign, why he’s being called before Congress to testify, why the SEC has reportedly launched a probe into Nvidia—you have to understand how the U.S. got locked in this AI race with China, and how Nvidia’s chips work to power the AI boom. You have to understand the policies that have led to the export restrictions on the chips that Nvidia sells, and the convoluted loopholes that Nvidia and Alice Huang have allegedly used to get chips into China. And my guest today: He not only understands every element of this story; he helps shape it. Ben Buchanan is the former White House special adviser on AI during the Biden administration. Buchanan helped design the chip-export controls on China that Huang and Nvidia lobbied against. And along with Tantum Collins, he’s the author of this new book, The Bitter Struggle: Superintelligence, Superpowers, and the Fate of the World . He was in the room for so many of the events that led to where we are now. And today, he’s going to help us mere mortals actually understand what the heck is going on with China, chips, Jensen Huang, the AI race, and crucially, why all of it matters. He joins me now. I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . [ Music ] Warzel: Ben Buchanan, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Ben Buchanan: Thanks for having me. Warzel: So I’m hoping in this interview that we could do some very basic questions that will lead to this deeper understanding of the U.S.-China race, the labs; what’s going on. But first I just want to ask about Jensen Huang. Have you taken what we know now and reexamined any of either the interactions you’ve had with him or his company? Like, were there things in retrospect that now that look like signs of vulnerability? How are you processing this news moment, given your relationship to this entire story? Buchanan: For background, I was the White House special adviser for AI and worked in the National Security Council, and was the architect of a lot of the chip controls that seem to be at the crux of this story here. In the course of doing that work for four years, we had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. Certainly about the importance of chips to national security, the importance of AI to national security, and the necessity to cut off smuggling routes and remote access routes for China to get access to that technology. So, in some sense, it’s like a new chapter in a long-running novel. Maybe a particularly salacious and interesting chapter. But it fits the themes of the novel that I’ve lived, I guess now for six years. Warzel: Some of this stuff, especially. And I want to get into the stuff about Megaspeed: the company that Huang’s alleged mistress, and alleged Chinese intelligence asset, worked for. That’s in your book. Megaspeed is in your book. And so I’m just curious. Like, was all this on your radar, and you were expecting it all to come out in some fashion? Or were you pretty shocked by the fact that we’re all talking about this right now? Buchanan: I never knew of the sex thing. As best I can recall, I did not know of Megaspeed in the government. I definitely don’t think I ever heard the name Alice Huang. Megaspeed is in the book because The New York Times did a good story on it 13 or 14 months ago. And it looked to us, when we were writing the book, as a great avatar or example of exactly the kind of smuggling and remote access we were worried about, and we were trying to prevent. While the particulars of this case are new to me, or at least were not something we discussed in the government, the general idea of circumvention of the export controls because this technology is so important was something that we spent a lot of time on and in fact were actively trying to combat. Warzel: So I wanna ask some basic questions here, because I imagine I’m not alone in what is essentially like a pretty shallow understanding of the story in Nvidia. I think, you know, reading the news, a lot of people understand they make advanced AI chips, power the boom we’re experiencing here. They have an extraordinary amount of market share. But walk me through just to set the table here. Like, why is that? What makes Nvidia’s chips so great, so necessary, such a fundamental part of this whole boom? Buchanan: I would look at Nvidia as a key part of maybe the world’s most advanced supply chain and manufacturing process. So Nvidia designs the chips that are incredibly intricate—hundreds of billions of transistors at nanometer scale—that enable this AI revolution that we’re part of, for better or for worse. And those chips are made in Taiwan almost exclusively at TSMC using equipment from ASML in the Netherlands. These are three companies we profile in a lot of detail in the book, because they’re three of the most important companies in the world. Everyone knows of Nvidia; some people know of TSMC; almost no one knows of ASML. But it’s that kind of supply chain, and then all their subcontractors from there, that is at the core of AI. In AI, we have this notion called the bitter lesson , which is the inspiration for the book’s title, The Bitter Struggle . And the bitter lesson is that AI scientists want to make AI systems almost in this divine-creation process, in which they’re handcrafting the algorithms to perfectly mimic or encapsulate human knowledge. But actually, what works much better, we’ve observed, is giving the systems a flexible algorithm from which to learn. A lot of computing power. And getting out of the way. And that’s why it’s computing power—and in particular these days, Nvidia’s chips—that are at the absolute forefront of this AI story, and therefore this geopolitical story. Because what companies have realized is they can scale up the amount of computing power. They can scale up the amount of Nvidia chips that are used to make AI systems, and they get much more powerful systems as a result. In a very predictable fashion. And that, more than any other single factor, I think, has been the tailwind that’s propelled AI progress over the last 10 or 15 years. Warzel: And it’s what’s made them these companies just basically insatiable, right? In terms of how much they want to purchase. How much they want to use. Buchanan: That’s right. Yeah, it’s worth dwelling, for one second, just on the numbers here. Because they’re absolutely mind blowing. And they underscore one of the other important elements in the book and in our policy—which is that AI is the first revolutionary technology of the last hundred or so years that comes from the private sector. Think about nukes and space, and so much else, coming from the government. The government’s cutting the checks at a minimum, and has some capacity to steer where the technology goes. The modern paradigm of AI, this computing power–driven paradigm that we were just talking about, comes from the private sector. And it really is just eye-popping: the amount of investment the private sector is making in pursuit of the bitter lesson, or what’s sometimes called the scaling law. In 2026 alone, the estimates are that the hyperscalers, the big compute companies, will spend $700 billion on infrastructure and growing to a trillion or so dollars by 2027. Just taking the 2026 number, that’s akin to a Manhattan Project basically every two or three weeks. That’s more than America spent building the entire interstate-highway system, adjusting for inflation over 35 years. So it’s just so hard to overestimate the amount of computing power at play here in making these AI systems. Warzel: And it sets the stakes of this, I think, extremely well. Before we get into the nuts and bolts of this Nvidia story, I wanna step back; talk to a little bit about our technological relationship to China. You’ve said in the book, in the past, that AI will be the fulcrum on which the U.S.-China rivalry turns. So help me understand why that is. And also why it’s so bad that China gets access to these chips. Buchanan: We entered the White House in 2021 with the belief that AI would become very relevant, if not at the absolute center, of national-security affairs. Not just with China, but around the world. There’s a number of ways in which that importance could manifest over time, which we thought would take five or so years. Let’s take the one that’s the most concrete right now, and that’s cyber operations. It’s no secret that the United States and China engage every single day in cyber operations; cyber espionage against one another. That this is one of the key contours of competition between the two nations—that if you have an advantage in cyber operations, you have a substantial national-security advantage. I don’t think anyone can test that at this point. What was speculative in 2021—but that we believed would come to pass before too long—was that AI would change cyber operations. In 2026, it has. In 2026 alone, AI systems have discovered thousands, if not tens of thousands, of critical vulnerabilities in vital software all over the internet. The AI companies that have built this software, working in concert with the U.S. government, have turned these vulnerabilities over to vendors and to other network defenders, so that they can be patched and remediated. Essentially making the internet as a whole more secure. My belief, and I think this is pretty well supported, is that if China had access to such a technology and was finding these kinds of vulnerabilities in software, it would not be turning them over to be fixed and remediated. It would be using them for intelligence purposes. And that would put key parts of American critical infrastructure at risk. Just recently, this past week, as we’re recording this here, an AI company using an advanced AI system disclosed that they had found a vulnerability in Java, one of the absolute core languages that makes the modern economy go. A couple of weeks ago, the same company announced that they found a vulnerability in PHP, which is the back end for 70 percent of the websites on the internet. So we are talking about mega-vulnerabilities that AI systems are finding that have profound national-security implications in the wrong hand. And our view was certainly that it was better for the United States to get to that threshold first. Warzel: So you’ve also said that this race to unlock all these capabilities, including the cyber capabilities, may be “winner take all,” I think is how you described it. Help me understand why that’s a zero-sum game. Buchanan: I think we should be very precise here. So the dynamics are close to winner take all—which is to say, if you get to these critical thresholds first, then you can aggregate for yourself a lot of the power that comes from reaching those thresholds. We just gave the cyber example. I think there’s no doubt that the nation that got there first has a lot of power. What you choose to do with that power does not need to be zero sum. And in fact, I would argue throughout American history, a lot of the moments where American policymaking was at its best was when it had a fair amount of power and in some ways ceded that power to institutions, or built a stabilizing framework. So I don’t know that it’s zero sum in the geopolitical sense. Certainly, when I was in the government, we spent a lot of time trying to negotiate with China. And trying to say to China: Look, we’re taking competitive actions here, of course. But we think there’s interest, and that both of us have, that are shared. Let’s work on making this a positive-sum relationship. The Chinese largely blew us off. We can talk about it if you’d like. But this was certainly a key part of our overall AI strategy. Warzel: How would you describe the “they blew us off” part of that? Buchanan: So in October 2023, President Biden signed an executive order that included a line that when you translate from the legalese, essentially, said the United States will engage on AI safety—not just with its allies and its partners, but with its competitors. And that of course meant China. And President Biden personally took that line to President Xi [Jinping] three weeks later when the two leaders met in Woodside, California. And essentially he said: I’m serious about this. We have to work together on this and have a positive-sum relationship . The two leaders agreed to set up a dialogue of the AI experts in Geneva in May of ’24. It happened. I was there. It was maybe 10 or so U.S.-government officials, 10 or so Chinese-government officials. We took it incredibly seriously. We sent essentially everyone who was an AI leader in the U.S. government, went on this trip. The Chinese did not. And the Chinese subordinated it to their political apparatus, and spent the entire meeting essentially saying, like: We’re not sure why you’re talking about risks. We don’t see risks in AI. All this discussion of risks, even shared risks, is American imperialism. We pushed anyway. And we said, No, we really think there’s shared risks here. We really think there’s things we can do that are positive sum. Eventually, after six months of pushing on that point, we got the most common-sense thing, the thing that you should think would take six minutes. And that was an agreement between the two leaders, President Biden and President Xi, when they met for the last time, in November 2024—to not put AI in nuclear command and control. And I think we can all agree we don’t want AI firing nuclear weapons. So this should be the most simple thing in the world, but it took 13 months of pushing to get China to even get there. I’m hopeful China’s posture is different now. Certainly if we had had a second term, we would have—we were making plans to continue outreach to China on this point. But there wasn’t a lot of doubt in my mind that China was not, at the time, ready to have a serious conversation about shared interests and shared risks, and how we could all work together. Warzel: Do you have any sense of where you think China sits now on this? Given that, you know, the capabilities have skyrocketed? This is clearly a more of a top-of-mind geopolitical issue probably than it was, you know, during the Biden administration. Buchanan: I can point to some pieces of evidence that suggests China’s taking it more seriously. There’s some suggestion they’re thinking about cyber risks and talking to their companies about cyber risks. There’s some suggestion in some of the Chinese Communist Party publications that they’re warning about the dangers of AI and so forth. So I think there’s some evidence. And certainly, those are the threads I would be pulling if I were in the government. But also, China is essentially a nation run by one person. And I think it’s very hard, you know, even when you have access to U.S. intelligence to know exactly what Xi Jinping is thinking. I don’t have access to U.S. intelligence right now. So I wouldn’t wanna pretend to know what’s in his head when it comes to AI. And that, really, at the end of the day is the ultimate question when it comes to China. [ Break ] Warzel: So the Biden White House has a, you know, very specific policy about China having access to Nvidia’s chips. There’s a real focus on this amongst all the AI-policy folks, including yourself. Take me to [Jensen] Huang and Nvidia. What is Huang’s policy toward China when it comes to selling to them or around this period? Buchanan: He said the same thing in private that he said in public. Which is, we put this policy in place in 2022. We said to him, essentially: The supply of chips in the world is fixed, because it’s so hard to make them. There’s not gonna be that many more coming off the line. And we want those chips to not go to China. Because we’re worried they’re gonna modernize their military; they’re gonna repress their population with these surveillance tools and the like. Instead, we want those chips to go to the rest of the world, but especially companies in democratic nations. And Nvidia’s posture was that this would really hurt them; that this was bad for them economically. And that they needed the China market in order to compete. And sometimes, to give the sort of steel man of Jensen’s position, Jensen would often say things like—or Jensen and, I should say, his supporters, because there’s a whole group of folks who had this view—would say things like: Well, we need to keep China dependent on American chips. And we’ve got to sell them the chips, so they don’t make their own. We disagreed with the two prongs of that argument. The first prong we disagreed with was that this would be very bad for Nvidia. And essentially, our view was that the bitter lesson that we talked about before was so dominant, that the tailwinds of demand for American compute—I think you said the companies in the United States are insatiable when it comes to compute. That’s absolutely right. Jensen said that as well. And they would buy every single chip Nvidia made, and they would buy it for a significant profit. And that’s exactly what happened. Nvidia’s market capitalization in 2022, when we did the controls, was something like $350 billion. Just before the Jensen scandal a couple of weeks ago, it was $5 trillion. They’ve had a rough week here. But depending on how you do the math, they’re probably up 10 or 15 X on where they were when the compute control started, because of the tailwind that we foresaw about the scaling law and the bitter lesson and the demand for compute. So Nvidia has done great. And in fact, on the Nvidia earnings call just this week, when asked about a recent Trump action to close some of these loopholes and reassert export controls, they downplayed the impact of it, because they’re now acknowledging the demand is so big around the world. So we don’t think we were hurting Nvidia. We think Nvidia was going to do very well under our policy, and indeed they did. The second question is: Are we hurting the United States? Because, do the chip controls cause China to indigenize production in a way they wouldn’t otherwise have? And therefore we lose some leverage over China because they’re no longer dependent on American chips? I also think this was wrong, and we thought it was wrong at the time. The reason why is that China knew the importance of advanced chips. As far back as 2014, when America was off fighting ISIS, China recognized, up to the Xi Jinping level and the State Council of China, recognized how important chipmaking was. China at the time was spending more money importing chips than it was spending importing oil. And they couldn’t make any advanced chips at home. So Xi Jinping began an effort when you count the public and private capital upwards of $200 billion to build a chipmaking industry in China. So they had the pedal to the metal on indigenization before we ever took any action. The Trump administration, in their first term, made it a little bit harder. They cut China off the top end of equipment called EV machines—from the company I mentioned before, ASML. And then when we took the controls, we put the controls in place in 2022 on chips. We also put controls in place on chipmaking equipment, another generation of chipmaking equipment, which were imperfect, but what held China back. So the bottom line is even today, even despite the controls and despite China’s more than a decade-long effort to indigenize, chipmaking is so hard that China has failed. And don’t take my word for it: [Commerce Secretary Howard] Lutnick, one of the men at the center of this recent export-control story, testified in 2025 China can make just 200,000 chips. And together, 200,000 for the whole country is not nearly enough. It’s not even enough for a single data center. So those were Nvidia’s arguments, and what our responses were to them. Warzel: So in 2022, as you said, the U.S. implements these pretty sweeping export controls on semiconductors or on the chips. Can you briefly explain to me that policy in broad source for people who are not familiar with, you know, the export controls? Buchanan: Basically, our view was the risk of diversion was so high—that the chips could be sold to a civilian buyer, but would end up in PLA, the Chinese-military data centers, or end up in the domestic surveillance apparatus—that we had to control the sale of chips. Not just to the particular military buyers in China, but to the whole country. So the policy in 2022, and then some tightenings thereafter, was to say to companies like Nvidia: You may not sell your product; these advanced chips. You can sell lower-end chips, but you cannot sell these particular advanced chips into China, full stop . And that was a big step. Warzel: This is a dumb question, but what’s the penalty there? Buchanan: It’s a crime. The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce have together pursued investigations to arrest and charge people who have violated U.S. export controls or smuggled chips into China, or things like that. Warzel: So the export controls, as I know it in the story, is ultimately one of the decisions that brings Huang and Nvidia—who are not, you know, huge political players leading up to this—more into the D.C. fold, right? It seems that a lot of like their advocacy, especially Huang’s, really ramps up in response to this. So I’m curious: Tell me how Nvidia started rolling up its sleeves and lobbying against those bans starting around 2022, when you guys put them in. Buchanan: We consulted with Nvidia as we were doing it, even before it happened. Because we were trying to understand the technology, and we were certainly not trying to surprise them out of the blue. So it’s not like they woke up one morning and said, Well, you know, the policy is in effect right now. So there were conversations all along. I think those conversations obviously intensified once the policy was in effect, and as we were making adjustments to it and so forth. But these were the reasonably standard conversations that the government has with companies. And you know, when I was the White House special adviser for AI, I talked to all the AI companies pretty regularly. I think it’s part of the job of the government, especially when the private sector is inventing the technology. It’s part of the job of the government to understand what they’re doing, and what its implications are. Warzel: But I’m curious. Like the tenor, the tone of it—as someone who had the opportunity to be in the room. I’ve seen some reports. There’s a report that I read recently from Semafor about Nvidia’s more recent lobbying efforts. Quoting an anonymous congressional staffer saying their MO has been largely gaslighting: creating an intense trust deficit between government, the Hill, and Nvidia. Like, were these conversations acrimonious? What’s the tenor of these conversations? Buchanan: I think they were strident, maybe even aggressive, but it didn’t bother me. I don’t—you know, I just felt like Jensen was doing his job, and talking his book. And those of us in the White House, and they were a group of us in the White House who had very strong conviction on this, felt like we were here to serve U.S. national security. And serve the public, and also serve American innovation. But we certainly felt like we had the technical depth to have detailed conversations with Nvidia, and we did. And you know, the policy ended where, I think, in general the policy should have ended. I would have probably been a little bit more aggressive, if you had asked me, in terms of some of the controls. But in general, I think the policy got to where it needed to be. Probably got there slower than it needed to get there. But in general, I’m happy with certainly our core strategic and technological thesis, which I think has been borne out at this point. Warzel: So now we’re at the current scandal. The affair with Alice Huang—no relation, and former executive at Megaspeed. Allegedly the Chinese intelligence asset. With the caveat that Megaspeed has denied all allegations of wrongdoing, can you explain a little bit about how this alleged chip smuggling works in practice? Buchanan: So I want to be clear here that I don’t have firsthand knowledge of Megaspeed. I’m only going off the news reports. I’ve left the U.S. government, obviously, in January 2025. But it does seem like Megaspeed is an exemplar of two categories of risk that worried us quite a bit when it comes to China’s access to chips. The first is that the chips themselves would be smuggled into China. So they would be purchased in a place like Malaysia or Singapore. There might be some facade of a buyer, potentially a company like Megaspeed in one of those places, that is taking the chips into their data center; is saying, Yes, we’re going to run them here. Everything is good. Don’t worry. And then they’re taking the chips out of the data center, and they’re shipping them into China. And they’re ending up in a Chinese-military data center or the data center of a company that works for the Chinese military, or something like that. And that obviously is a very significant concern for the United States, because that’s direct smuggling of the chips themselves. And we don’t know—once they go into China, we don’t know what the chips are going to be used for. The second category of concern is what’s called remote access. The chips still go to a kind of shady company in Malaysia or Singapore, or a place like that. They go into a data center, but they stay there. The difference is China—Chinese military, Chinese companies—just access that data center remotely over the internet. So the chips stay there, but China can train their next-frontier AI system on this data center, remote. So it’s a different way of circumvent export controls. And we made a decision in one of the export-control updates to try to block that. To say: As a condition of taking these chips, you have to pledge that you will not use them to enable Chinese AI training. President Trump, when he came into office, declined to enforce that rule. So there’s at least a legal gray space—of maybe it was permitted, or the administration wasn’t enforcing it. But those are the two big categories of concern: the actual physical smuggling of the chip, and then the remote access. It’s worth saying Nvidia spent a great deal of time in 2025 and 2026, including Jensen personally, saying chip smuggling is not an issue. And I think it’s obviously incorrect. Not just because of the Megaspeed case, but also because of other cases in which the Department of Justice has brought really well-documented indictments and criminal charges against people for smuggling chips in the way that I described. Warzel: In terms of that remote access to those data centers that are outside of China, for training purposes, it’s known that China has distilled—or sort of reverse-engineered, you know—U.S. models in order to kind of keep up in the race here. Is that where that is happening in your mind? Like, inside those places? Or is that happening more locally? Or is it a mix of the two? Buchanan: Assume it’s a mix. So let’s just be very precise about what’s happening. Distillation is a process in which you can essentially—you know, if folks here are Formula 1 fans, you can draft behind the car in front of you. And you can get the outputs of a leading AI system and come up with the facsimile of that system, imperfectly. You’ll lag capabilities, but it’s cheaper. That is a general concern. And one of the ways in which China has been trying to compensate for the lack of computing power. Essentially, is copying the Americans’ homework. That process of distillation still requires some computing power. And I would imagine China is using whatever computing power it has available to do the process of distillation, whether that’s chips overseas or chips in China. Companies have gotten much better at stopping distillation. So Anthropic, a company that I advise, but I don’t speak for, reported that they came up with methods in the summer of 2026 to stop distillation. I think it was like up to like 99 percent. And I think OpenAI is making some moves in that direction as well. So my suspicion, hard to know for sure, is that we will look at this kind of adversarial distillation as an artifact of a period from 2025 to 2026 where China really struggled with access to computing power, in part due to the export controls, and was using distillation as a way to try to keep up with the frontier. But I don’t think that will be sustainable for them in the long run. And then they’ll be back to the same box of not having enough computing power. [ Break ] Warzel: Given what we’ve learned about Megaspeed, and what you’ve said about the Department of Justice also bringing cases about people trying to, you know, navigate around these export controls—what is your sense of just how much Nvidia helped China get access to these chips? Like, how bad is this going to get for Jensen, for Nvidia, in terms of where this can go? Buchanan: It’s a great question. Again, I don’t have firsthand knowledge of the facts here, and I don’t want to pretend. It does seem like the amount of chips going through these channels was really significant, potentially even more than the number of chips China could make as a whole country itself. I think The Wall Street Journal reported something like $12 billion of chips. I’ve seen other reportings saying it was $4 billion to $5 billion of chips. Megaspeed is just one company. There were other companies that were potentially doing this. What Nvidia knew, what Jensen knew—that is all for congressional and maybe criminal investigators to find out. I don’t pretend to know. But certainly, as a national-security matter, I do think that the flow of chips to China in this way—smuggling and through remote data centers—is one of the biggest national-security weaknesses the United States has. And what you’ve seen really is a pretty clear bipartisan consensus to change the policy. And there’s bipartisan bills in the Congress—introduced by, you know, MAGA senators like Tom Cotton and Jim Banks, and people like that—that would cut China off chips and chipmaking equipment as a matter of law. So the president couldn’t change it, even if he wanted to. And then, even the Trump administration, this past Monday, changed their policy and cut off remote access to data centers and required licenses for shipments to Southeast Asia to try to cut off the smuggling. They’re not quite done; there’s still a couple loopholes in their rule. But that was a very significant action for an administration that really, you know, from the middle of 2025 to today, was only taking export controls away and not enforcing them, rather than putting them into practice. Warzel: So there are calls from Silicon Valley right—from the shareholders, from the, you know, VC types, the other tech founders of some esteem. They want Jensen Huang to come back. He’s a visionary; he’s integral to the AI economy . Help me understand the rationale here, because China is enemy No. 1 in terms of the race to superintelligence. But also, it just seems like they’re abandoning the China fears all of a sudden, or excusing this dalliance. This potential dalliance. Buchanan: I think a lot of the folks who are making those calls—which, to be clear, the Nvidia board pretty clearly rejected on their earnings call this week. A lot of that constellation of people has been pretty dismissive of the China concern. So they’re often the ones supporting selling chips to China. So at least they’re consistent on that front, in that they’re just not worried about this. I think there’s probably a key difference between my view and their view. Which is: I think AI really is going to matter for national security. And at least their revealed preference is they don’t think that, because they’re willing to let China in the game. But as a national-security matter, I certainly am very concerned and think these activities should be investigated. Warzel: What is so hard for me to understand with that is that the national-security imperative is part of the imperative of the companies, that are saying: We can’t afford to truly pace the frontier— or “stop” or “pause” or whatever —because it’s imperative that we beat China to this. I mean, I do feel like they’re speaking out of both corners of their mouth here. Buchanan: I do think, yeah. So if what you’re saying is sometimes the same people who are saying We can’t regulate AI are also saying Let’s sell chips to China. I mean: We can’t regulate AI, because we have to beat China are also saying Let’s sell chips to China . I agree. That is totally incoherent. It doesn’t make any sense to me. President Trump himself—in, you know, militaristic terms that I would not use, given our discussion before about how we hope to have a positive-sum outcome here—President Trump is very fond of saying: Whoever wins AI, wins . You would think if that is your policy, you would not want to sell chips to China. I don’t get it. I think it’s incoherent for the reason you describe. To be clear about what I do believe, my view is: American companies in fact do have to slow down. And I support pacing the frontier. We haven’t talked about it, but you know, part two of the book is all about how we regulated the AI companies, and what more we need to do on the regulation side. That was sort of huge part of our policy. And my view is that, in fact, the way in which we can create the space for regulation—as far back as 2021, we believed—was to slow China down. And China’s absolute dependence on American computing power was a way for us to slow China down, to build a lead for the United States. And then to, if you’d like, spend that lead on safety, to when the technology got to a critical moment. Which is what we’re in right now. To regulate the companies pretty aggressively, if I had my way. To make sure this technology is safe before it’s rolled out. Without this argument of: Well, we’re in an arms race with China; we must forge ahead . Which I thought was just very destructive. Warzel: So where does this all leave us right now, as we’re sitting in the story here? We’re talking Wednesday, November 18th. Obviously, things are changing by the minute. How dangerous and serious is this for Nvidia, as Huang goes to testify before Congress in December? Like, what are the stakes for both Huang and Nvidia going forward? Buchanan: I think they’re very high. Congress, in a bipartisan way, said it’s gonna do an investigation here. I don’t know what’s gonna turn up, but certainly they’ve got a lot of threads to pull. Whether or not there’s a criminal investigation, I have no idea. But I do suspect there will be a lot of government investigations into what happened here, and there should be. I guess in the medium term, Nvidia’s chips are still gonna be really good, and there’s still gonna be big demand for them. So as long as Nvidia can keep making great products, I think they will continue to sell those products. I guess it’s an open question of: Can they make great products without Jensen? We’ll see. They’ve got 31,000 research engineers, or something like that. So there’s a lot of smart people there, and they’ve got a lot of great technology. So we’ll see what happens to them technologically. But yeah; in the context of the investigations, certainly I would describe this as a serious moment. Warzel: What should senators be asking? Or what should anyone in Congress be asking Huang when he’s up there, you know, in front of Congress? Buchanan: It’s the most important, age-old question in any kind of D.C. investigation, which is: What did you know, and when did you know it? And they should be asking Jensen that, and they should be asking the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, that. Who knew what about where these chips were going. Who was getting them. How active was Nvidia’s role in enabling smuggling? How active was Jensen’s role? Again, I don’t have firsthand knowledge of the answers. But those were all the questions I’d be asking. Warzel: And I think lastly here, what has this done for the AI ecosystem right now? Like, is it in a worse place than it was? Or let’s just say, the American AI ecosystem? Is it in a worse place than it was two weeks ago, before all of this stuff really trickled out into the press? Or it was about the same? Buchanan: I think it probably creates some turbulence in the waters, but my suspicion is we’ll look back at this in six or 12 months, and the big story of AI will be largely unchanged by this. And the big story of AI, you know—as we spent a lot of detail on the book—is: You have really powerful chips being used by really capable algorithms, at larger and larger scales. Yielding extraordinarily capable systems, with profound national-security implications and profound implications for everyday life and democratic values. That story. To be clear, I’m not a cheerleader for that story. You know, you don’t write a book called The Bitter Struggle if you’re a cheerleader. But I think that story is largely undiminished by these events here. Warzel: What about China? Where are they better off? Are they worse off than they were? Buchanan: They’re worse off. They’re absolutely worse off. Because there was a bipartisan consensus that was forming on denying China access to computing power. But they had big allies that were saying, You know, let’s sell China the chips . And those allies were having some success. Chief amongst some, Jensen. David Sacks, Trump’s—my successor, as you know—AI adviser to the president, was advocating for this, at least based on the reporting. President Trump had advocated for in some context. And now the bipartisan consensus has, at least so far, started to harden against them. That is bad for China’s access to compute, and ultimately that is bad for China. Warzel: Ben Buchanan: Thank you for coming and helping to demystify this; talking about it in these very plain terms. I wanna have you back on, to talk about the regulation part of this, later. But this has been very helpful. Buchanan: It is great to talk about this subject, and it’s great to have interest in this subject of the chips and chip controls. Because this is a wonky subject for sure—that now has gotten this gloss of a sex scandal and a spy story. But I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say this is one of the most important subjects in the world for U.S. national policy. Warzel: And we’ll keep following it. Thank you very much, Ben, for coming on. Buchanan: Thanks for having me. [ Music ] Warzel: If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, or on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work, and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. content:
﻿ 以下是上周西太平洋主要舰船活动和演习的摘要。 2026 年 11 月 11 日，新加坡，隶属第 13 海军陆战队远征部队海军陆战队中型倾转旋翼机中队 (VMM) 364（增援）的一名美国海军陆战队员正在准备一架 MV-22B 鱼鹰，以便在黄蜂级两栖攻击舰马金岛号 (LHD-8) 上起飞。美国海军陆战队照片周五，两栖攻击舰马金岛号根据当地船舶观察员和 AIS 数据，两栖船坞运输舰 LHD-8（LHD-8）和两栖船坞运输舰 USS John P. Murtha（LPD-26）已驶入新加坡三巴旺。马金岛号和约翰·P·穆萨号与两栖运输船坞舰安克雷奇号 (LPD-23) 和已上船的第 13 海军陆战队远征部队组成了马金岛两栖待命大队。安克雷奇仍停靠在日本横须贺司令舰队活动中心。 2026 年 11 月 14 日，美国海军水手长三等大副马修·普里米蒂沃（左）和水手长二等大副杰伦·斯罗克莫顿在新加坡海上抛锚期间将千斤顶杆固定在独立型濒海战斗舰塔尔萨号（LCS-16）上。美国海军照片濒海战斗舰塔尔萨号（LCS-16）驶入新加坡周六出发，周一出发。塔尔萨隶属于第七驱逐舰中队（DESRON），该中队部署在东南亚前沿，是东南亚行动区指定舰艇的主要战术和作战指挥官。
在菲律宾马尼拉，澳大利亚总理安东尼·艾博内塞于 2026 年 11 月 15 日在菲律宾马尼拉参观澳大利亚皇家海军舰队加油船 HMAS Stalwart (A304)。澳大利亚国防军照片 澳大利亚皇家海军舰队加油船 HMAS Stalwart (A304) 对马尼拉进行港口访问。周日，正在出席东南亚国家联盟（ASEAN）峰会的澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴内斯（Anthony Albanese）访问了这艘船，会见了船员和在菲律宾的澳大利亚国防军人员。 Stalwart 正在进行区域部署。 2026 年 11 月 16 日，南海，美国海军燃气轮机系统技术员（机械）海员谢恩·文森特（来自肯塔基州）在南海将军区斑马训练期间，对阿利·伯克级导弹驱逐舰拉尔夫·约翰逊号 (DDG-114) 上的通道中的斑马配件进行注释。美国海军照片 驱逐舰拉尔夫·约翰逊号（DDG-114）于周日穿越吕宋海峡，截至周一正在南海作业。拉尔夫·约翰逊（Ralph Johnson）前沿部署并分配到日本基地的DESRON 15。在越南海防，法国海军护卫舰FS Vendémiaire（F734）周一与越南海岸警卫队8004号近海巡逻船进行了联合搜救演习。此次演习是在法国护卫舰于11月12日开始访问海防后离开海防之后进行的。 Vendémiaire 总部位于新喀里多尼亚努美阿。
在菲律宾海 中国人民解放军海军辽宁舰仍部署在菲律宾海。该打击群最后一次被目击是在10月份，包括航母辽宁号（16）、巡洋舰鞍山号（101）和无锡号（104）以及驱逐舰淮南号（123）。此后随行船只可能发生了变化。在釜山，韩国皇家海军近海巡逻舰 HMS Spey (P234) 于 2026 年 11 月 16 日抵达韩国釜山进行港口访问。英国皇家海军照片 英国皇家海军近海巡逻舰 HMS Spey (P234) 周一抵达釜山进行港口访问。斯佩号和姊妹舰添马舰 (P233) 正在前沿部署

Murtha (LPD-26) pulled into Sembawang, Singapore , according to local ship spotters and AIS data. Makin Island and John P. Murtha , with amphibious transport dock USS Anchorage (LPD-23) and the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, form the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group. Anchorage remains docked at Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka in Japan. U.S. Navy Boatswain’s Mate 3rd Class Matthew Primitivo (left) and Boatswain’s Mate 2nd Class Jaron Throckmorton attach the jack staff aboard the Independence-variant littoral combat ship USS Tulsa (LCS-16) during sea and anchor in Singapore, Nov. 14, 2026. US Navy photo Littoral Combat Ship USS Tulsa (LCS-16) pulled into Singapore on Saturday and departed on Monday . Tulsa is assigned to Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 7, which is forward deployed in Southeast Asia and is the primary tactical and operational commander of assigned ships in the Southeast Asia area of operations. In Manila, Philippines Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visits Royal Australian Navy fleet oiler HMAS Stalwart (A304) on Nov. 15, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. Australian Defense Force photo Royal Australian Navy fleet oiler HMAS Stalwart (A304) carried out a port visit to Manila. On Sunday , Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who was in town for the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit, visited the ship to meet with the crew and Australian Defense Force personnel in the Philippines. Stalwart is conducting a regional presence deployment. In the South China Sea U.S. Navy Gas Turbine Systems Technician (Mechanical) Seaman Shane Vincent, from Kentucky, annotates zebra fittings in a passageway aboard Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Ralph Johnson (DDG-114) during general quarters zebra training in the South China Sea, Nov. 16, 2026. US Navy photo Destroyer USS Ralph Johnson (DDG-114) was operating in the South China Sea as of Monday , having transited the Luzon Strait on Sunday . Ralph Johnson forward-deployed and assigned to Japan based DESRON 15. In Haiphong, Vietnam French Navy frigate FS Vendémiaire (F734) on Monday conducted a joint search and rescue exercise with Vietnam Coast Guard offshore patrol vessel 8004. The exercise followed the French frigate’s departure from Haiphong after a port visit that began on Nov. 12 . Vendémiaire is based in Noumea, New Caledonia. In the Philippine Sea The People’s Liberation Army Navy Liaoning CSG remains deployed in the Philippine Sea. The strike group was last visually sighted in October and included aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16) cruisers CNS Anshan (101) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainan (123). The accompanying ships may have since changed. In Busan, South Korea Royal Navy offshore patrol vessel HMS Spey (P234) arrived Nov. 16, 2026, in Busan, South Korea, for a port visit. Royal Navy photo Royal Navy offshore patrol vessel HMS Spey (P234) arrived on Monday in Busan for a port visit. Spey and sister ship HMS Tamar (P233) are forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific. Near Honshu, Japan Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182) and Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri (F49) near Honshu, Japan, on Nov. 13, 2026. JMSDEF photo Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182) and Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri (F49) conducted the Japan-India Maritime Exercise (JAIMEX) 26 in waters south of Honshu from Nov. 13 to Saturday . The two ships carried out tactical maneuvering, communication and crossdeck drills. Sahyadri is making its way home after participating in Exercise Malabar 2026, which ran from Nov 5-12 in the waters off Yokosuka. In the East China Sea Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) on Nov. 15, 2026, in the East China Sea. Royal Canadian Navy photo Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) carried out a passing exercise with Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri in the East China Sea on Sunday . Regina is on deployment under Operation Horizon, the Canadian Armed Forces forward presence deployment to the Indo-Pacific and Operation Neon, the country’s surveillance and monitoring operations on North Korean maritime sanctions violations. The Royal Canadian Navy frigate carried out Operation Neon from late September to early November . Stuart docked in Yokosuka on Nov. 12 following its participation in Exercise Malabar 2026. Submarine tender USS Frank Cable (AS-40) departed on Monday from CFAY, according to local ship spotters. Frank Cable pulled into CFAY on Nov. 11 for a port visit. Amphibious transport dock USS Anchorage , which has been anchored offshore since Nov. 11, moved into CFAY following Frank Cable’s departure, according to local ship spotters . Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina arrived in Yokosuka on Thursday for a port visit. Fast attack submarine USS Toledo (SSN-769) pulled into CFAY on Tuesday , according to local shipspotters. In the Miyako Strait PLAN destroyer CNS Qiqihar (121) and fleet oiler CNS Chaohu (890) on Nov. 16, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo PLAN destroyer CNS Qiqihar (121) and fleet oiler CNS Chaohu (890) were spotted Monday sailing north 60 kilometers – 37 miles – west of Kume Island, having previously transited between Okinawa and Miyako Island to exit the Philippine Sea. A JMSDF P-3C Orion Maritime Patrol Aircraft shadowed the PLAN ships. Japan’s Joint Staff Office (JSO) noted that Qiqihar has traveled back and forth in Japan’s southwest region since Oct. 17 when it transited the Osumi Strait to enter the Pacific Ocean and then returned to the East China Sea through the Miyako Strait on Nov. 1. On Nov. 2, the PLAN destroyer sailed through the Miyako Strait to enter the Philippine Sea and returned the same way back into the East China Sea on Nov. 4. On Nov. 12, Qiqihar again sailed through the Miyako Strait to enter the Philippine Sea. The JSO also noted that Chaohu sailed south through the Miyako Strait to enter the Philippine Sea on Nov. 2. In the East China Sea A Chinese Y-9 electronic intelligence aircraft on Nov. 16, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo On Monday, a Chinese Y-9 electronic intelligence aircraft flew in from China and conducted a patrol circuit across the East China Sea, covering an area extending from south of the Danjo Islands to northwest of the island of Amami Oshima before returning to China. In response, the Japan Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter aircraft from the Southwestern Air Defense Command and other units. A Chinese TB-001 reconnaissance/attack Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) on Nov. 19, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo On Thursday, a Chinese TB-001 reconnaissance/attack Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) flew in from China and over the East China Sea as far as the waters southwest of the Danjo Islands and proceeded southwest. The drone flew west of Okinawa before returning to China. The JASDF scrambled fighter aircraft from the Southwestern Air Defense Command in response. In the Sea of Japan A Russian Tu-95 bomber on Nov. 17, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo Russian aircraft violated Japanese territorial airspace on two occasions and prompted fighter aircraft scrambles as they entered the Air Defense Identification Zones (ADIZs) of Japan, South Korea and Taiwan on Tuesday. The three countries initially did not provide specifics of the Russian aircraft but later released the flights were conducted by two Tu-95MS bombers and two IL-76 transports, which landed in Vietnam that same day. One Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace northwest of the island of Okinoshima. A second aircraft violated Japanese airspace in the same area minutes later. The two Tu-95MS bombers returned to Russia on Thursday, first passing through the Taiwan Air Defense Identification Zone. Republic of China Air Force fighter aircraft shadowed the Russian bombers. From morning to afternoon, the bombers flew in the airspace between Taiwan and Yonaguni Island. The aircraft flew over the East China Sea where they were joined by two Russian Tu-142 MPAs, which had flown in from the Sea of Japan and through the Tsushima Strait. The joint air group then flew through the Tsushima Strait to return to Russia. The JASDF scrambled fighter aircraft in response. In Vladivostok, Russia Russian Navy improved Kilo-class attack submarine RFS Yakutsk (B-610) arrived Nov. 13 at its new homeport of Vladivostok to join the Russian Navy Pacific Fleet. “The submarine completed an inter-fleet passage from the Baltic Fleet to the Pacific Fleet via the Northern Sea Route, covering more than 9,000 nautical miles,” reads a news release by the fleet. Yakutsk was built in St. Petersburg and commissioned into the Russian Navy Pacific Fleet in June of 2025. Japan previously tracked Yakutsk with amphibious landing ship RFS Nikolai Vilkov (081) and tugboat Fotiy Krylov on Nov. 10 as they transited La Pérouse Strait to enter the Sea of Japan. In Auckland, New Zealand USCGC Harriet Lane (WMEC-903) in Auckland, New Zealand, on Nov. 15, 2026. Royal New Zealand Navy photo Coast Guard Cutter USCGC Harriet Lane (WMEC-903) participated in Exercise Maru 26, a Proliferation Security Initiative exercise that ran from Monday to Wednesday in Auckland, New Zealand. Harriet Lane arrived in Auckland on Sunday and conducted drills with Royal New Zealand Navy patrol vessel HMNZS Taupo (P3570). Around 150 personnel from 30 countries participated in Maru 26, which was focused on countering the illicit trafficking of weapons of mass destruction and related materials. This post was written by Dzirhan Mahadzir.

title: 特朗普习近平深圳峰会 台湾议题未见新说法

content: 唐纳德·特朗普总统抵达深圳宝安国际机场准备出席亚太经合组织(APEC)峰会和美中双边以及美中俄三边会谈，中国国家主席习近平在机场迎接。(2026年11月18日) 华盛顿 — 美国总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)星期四(11月19日)在深圳与中国国家主席习近平举行了双边会晤。根据中方会后的声明，特朗普在会谈中表明了美国“不支持”台独的立场；习近平则要美方在台湾问题上“做正确的事”，避免美中关系出现大波折。美方至截稿前尚未有关于美中元首峰会的正式声明或会谈纪要。 特朗普总统在出席亚太经合组织(APEC)领导人峰会时与习近平举行了双边会谈。根据中国外交部发布的声明，习近平在会中表示，他与特朗普“共同探索中美两个大国正确相处之道，确立了‘中美建设性战略稳定关系’的新定位”，两国关系“总体稳定向好”。 声明说，习近平还提到，“中美元首外交的引领作用不可替代”，强调要延续两国关系目前的稳定向好势头，“关键是要在落实元首共识上付诸行动”，并称一时解决不了的分歧要建设性管控以防止矛盾升级。“在台湾问题上，美方要坚持做正确的事，避免中美关系出现大波折。” 此外，声明中也有一段描述特朗普的发言称，特朗普提及他与习近平保持密切交往，友谊日益深厚，共同引领美中关系发展，双方应保持美中关系稳定发展势头，公平处理好各自关切，并称“美国不支持‘台独’。” 美国之音向白宫和国务院寻求关于美中元首会谈的声明，以及对特朗普总统在关于台湾议题上的相关陈述请求置评，白宫提供了美中俄领导人三方在会谈后发表的四点和平宣言，其中并未提及台湾。记者至发稿前尚未收白宫或国务院其他相关回复。 在美国国会，参议院外委会民主党首席参议员珍妮·沙欣(Jeanne Shaheen)与其他八位同党议员，星期三在特朗普与习近平会面前发表的联合声明中，敦促特朗普在深圳的两国元首峰会中依据《台湾关系法》及“六项保证”重申美国对台湾的承诺。 “他必须直面中国对台湾的军事恫吓，并通过依法行事向台湾提供140亿美元此前已批准的军售，重申我们在《台湾关系法》及‘六项保证’之下对台湾的承诺，”声明说。 美国智库保卫民主基金会(FDD)中国项目高级主任克雷格·辛格尔顿(Craig Singleton)在给美国之音的电邮中说，特朗普在与习近平的双边会谈中将两人的个人关系视为应对危机的一种“保险”，但习近平却希望通过这种个人关系换取美国在台湾议题上的克制。 “在他与习近平的双边交往中，特朗普将个人关系视为应对一个危机时的保险，认为两国领导人能在他们的国家激烈竞争的同时依然保持冷静。习近平正试图通过确保美国在台湾议题上的克制来兑现这个保险，”辛格尔顿说。 他说，习近平在两人的会谈中要求美方落实先前的元首“共识”，正是意图通过两人的个人关系，换取特朗普在台湾议题上的克制，特别是在对台军售上的议题上。 “他在他们的双边会面中敦促要落实两国领导人此前达成的‘共识’，意图将台湾议题上的外交模糊转为新的政策预期，尤其是在军售方面。特朗普很可能将当前军售的延迟视为暂时的停顿，而习近平则越来越将其视为一个先例。这种认知差异持续的时间越长，在不引发特朗普希望避免的危机的情况下恢复军售就越困难。 截至发稿时尚未见到台北方面对美中元首第三次峰会的正式反应。 台湾陆委会发言人梁文杰在星期四的例行记者会上说，台湾并非此次特朗普与习近平的会谈重点，详细情况台湾政府会持续掌握。 台湾中央社报道，陆委会副主委梁文杰在记者会上针对特习会是否谈及台湾，以及台湾政府对特习会对台海影响的评估表示，台湾并非此次会谈重点，较重要的大概是乌克兰停火及伊朗核武的问题，即便台湾议题被提到也“可能是比较边缘性的话题”，详细情况还有待进一步掌握。 他说，无论是特习会或美中俄三方元首会晤，时间都相对有限，而且三方各自想要的东西都不同，关注的重点也不一样，实际上要有任何具体成果都蛮困难，“我想这一次应该不会涉及到台湾议题”。

title: 台湾九合一大选｜中共介选不只为胜选 更为了使台湾社会陷入分裂
summary: 台湾学者警示，中共介选其实不仅针对特定候选人及关键选区，也可能透过长期资讯操作，加剧台湾政治对立，侵蚀民众对选举公平性与民主制度的信任。真正需要防范的，不只是谁当选、谁落选，而是台湾社会是否正在不知不觉中陷入了猜疑与分裂。 距离台湾2026九合一选举投票100天。民进党台北市长参选人沈伯洋（前中）21日上午赴内湖碧湖公园扫街，沈伯洋会后与民进党台北市议员何孟桦（前左1）、王孝维（后右2）、议员参选人陈又新（后左2）、高嘉瑜（前右）等人一同受访，回应有关国民党北市议员全区配票等
content: 台湾学者警示，中共介选其实不仅针对特定候选人及关键选区，也可能透过长期资讯操作，加剧台湾政治对立，侵蚀民众对选举公平性与民主制度的信任。真正需要防范的，不只是谁当选、谁落选，而是台湾社会是否正在不知不觉中陷入了猜疑与分裂。 距离台湾2026九合一选举投票100天。民进党台北市长参选人沈伯洋（前中）21日上午赴内湖碧湖公园扫街，沈伯洋会后与民进党台北市议员何孟桦（前左1）、王孝维（后右2）、议员参选人陈又新（后左2）、高嘉瑜（前右）等人一同受访，回应有关国民党北市议员全区配票等议题。 © 中央社记者翁睿坤摄 广告 随着2026年九合一选举进入倒数关键期，各界对中共介入选举的方式与目的也越加关注。然而，中共介选其实不仅针对特定候选人及关键选区，也可能透过长期资讯操作，加剧台湾政治对立，侵蚀民众对选举公平性与民主制度的信任。 学者同时警告，真正需要防范的，不只是谁当选、谁落选，而是台湾社会是否正在不知不觉中陷入了猜疑与分裂。 中共介选手段 台湾自1996年首次总统直选以来，中共介入台湾选举的手段不断演变，从早期军事威吓、政治施压与经济利诱，逐步扩展至境外资金渗透、在地人际网络、网军操作、真假讯息混杂，以及AI生成短影音。 根据《中央广播电台》报导，亚洲政经与和平交流协会在10月主办的「选战倒数！中共介选手法与台湾民主防卫」座谈会中提到，国安局公布的最新报告显示，中共疑似已提前为年底选举展开情报搜集及网路侵扰准备，不仅透过AI、假帐号、网路水军等手段操作舆论，更锁定台湾能源、食安、国防及候选人政见等议题散布争议讯息。 国安情报团队统计，今年1月至9月已搜报超过250万则争议讯息，较去年同期增加近5成，其中脸书与脆（Threads）的占比明显增加，成为中共操作认知作战的主要管道。此外，政府网路服务网每日平均遭侵扰高达258万余次，7月单月更达1亿8,560万余次。 出席座谈会的陆委会副主委沉有忠分析中共介选手段是「软硬兼施」，无论是对特定阵营释放利多，或是对不希望看到当选的阵营恐吓、跨国镇压，都是中共介选的一环。以同时并用胡萝卜和棍棒的方法，来进行促统、促容、反独、反介入。一方面用所谓的惠台措施来推动促统、促容，另一方面用军事胁迫、外交打压，甚至是内部的一些跨境镇压的方式，来进行反独跟反干涉的这个部分。 沉有忠表示，未来不排除中共会使用更多AI手段、深伪假影音，以抹黑特定阵营候选人、散播争议讯息的方式介入台湾选举。 事实上，花莲县长参选人魏嘉贤就曾在10月底指控，有人组织性利用境外社群帐号介入花莲选举、操弄舆论，不排除涉及境外势力。他指出，社群平台脆在8月出现所在地显示为香港的帐号，发布支持花莲县长特定候选人的助选讯息，遭网友发现后随即下架。脸书粉丝专页也突然涌入大量僵尸帐号，留下AI生成的重复、攻击性留言及大量「怒」表情符号。经检视这些帐号平时多发布与非洲、中东、东南亚等地相关的内容，名称多使用外国文字，头像也大多为外国人物。遭质疑背后恐有组织性操作，刻意利用这些境外帐号操弄网路舆论。 中共介选目的在加剧台湾政治极化 美国圣汤玛斯大学国际研究讲座教授叶耀元曾向媒体表示，看待中共介选问题，应放在更广泛的对台认知作战框架下理解。外界往往将介选目的简化为支持特定政党或打击特定候选人，但这只是表面效果。从长期战略来看，中共更可能利用政治争议与资讯操弄，加深不同阵营的敌意，让台湾人民逐渐失去对彼此及民主程序的信任。 叶耀元认为，这些事件不一定达到中共原先期待的效果，甚至可能产生反作用。但也显示对台影响并不限于选举期间的个别操作，而是可能透过更大规模的政治事件，改变台湾民众对安全、两岸关系及未来发展的判断。 他也指出，假讯息与政治讯息操弄能否直接改变选民投票行为，并没有外界想像中简单。选民原有的政党认同、政治立场及价值观，都会影响他们对同一事件的解读。对原本支持不同政党的人而言，相同讯息可能带来截然不同的结论。 并且很多时候，这种介选或资讯作战的结果，就是「蓝的更蓝、绿的更绿」。叶耀元表示，符合既有立场的讯息，可能进一步强化支持者的判断，却未必能说服原本立场不同的人。至于平时不关心政治、不经常接触新闻的民众，是否接收到相关讯息，也不能单凭社群平台上的讨论热度推断。 因此中共介选真正值得警惕的，不只是某则假讯息是否改变选票，而是长期操作能否使政治敌意持续升高，让民众逐渐以「非黑即白」的方式理解政治，甚至不再相信选举制度能公平反映人民意志。 沈伯洋成为中共介选首要施压对象 战争研究所（ISW）与美国企业研究所（AEI）共同撰发的最新一期《中国与台湾情势更新》（The China & Taiwan Update）报告指出，北京当局近期升级对所谓「顽固台独分子」的胁迫策略。报告点出民进党台北市长参选人沈伯洋近来成为中共首要施压对象。 报告分析，中国国台办继2024年将沈伯洋列入「台独顽固分子」后，在10月又宣布对沈伯洋父亲名下的VWAY公司祭出制裁。再以香港亲中的《文汇报》与《大公报》配合先行披露相关内容，紧接着国台办隔天即宣布制裁。台湾陆委会对此严厉批评中方正刻意介入选举。 此外，沈伯洋也曾在10月发生遭AI冒用声音并于社群平台上流传事件，内容捏造涉及「美国军购回扣」等言论，被刻意包装成私下谈话外流。但假音档中出现「岛内」等中国惯用语，遭网友与团队识破，经调查发现帐号来自境外。 作者： 台北特约记者 陈筱涵

title: 美國會對華年度報告出爐：AI、芯片與數據安全成重點
summary: 美國華盛頓國會大廈外景。 (Aaron Schwartz/Reuters) 美國國會美中經濟與安全審查委員會（USCC）11月18日公佈《2026年度國會報告》，向國會提出30項建議，其中10項為重點建議。 科技議題更加突出 該年度報告分為四大部分、十個章節，涵蓋美中經貿與外交安全、中國在印太及拉丁美洲的活動、海底競爭、大宗商品市場，以及數據、半導體、人工智能、臺灣和香港等議題。 與2025年的報告相比，今年的報告建議由28項增至30項，專題研究則從製造業創新、能源及太空競爭
content: 美國華盛頓國會大廈外景。 (Aaron Schwartz/Reuters) 美國國會美中經濟與安全審查委員會（USCC）11月18日公佈《2026年度國會報告》，向國會提出30項建議，其中10項為重點建議。 科技議題更加突出 該年度報告分為四大部分、十個章節，涵蓋美中經貿與外交安全、中國在印太及拉丁美洲的活動、海底競爭、大宗商品市場，以及數據、半導體、人工智能、臺灣和香港等議題。 與2025年的報告相比，今年的報告建議由28項增至30項，專題研究則從製造業創新、能源及太空競爭等領域，轉向更加突出數據資源、AI技術體系、印度及海底戰略競爭。 經濟與供應鏈：關注貿易失衡及關鍵藥品 報告認為，中國經濟仍面臨內需疲弱、房地產低迷及製造業產能過剩等問題，預計2026年商品貿易順差可能連續第二年超過1萬億美元。 在供應鏈方面，委員會提出與印度合作，利用長期採購承諾和投資支持，減少美國對中國原料藥及關鍵起始原料的依賴，並加強監測中國大宗商品交易市場。 人工智能與芯片：建議強化審查 在人工智能領域，委員會認為，中國開放權重AI模型在美國的應用可能涉及數據與網絡安全風險，主張對關鍵基礎設施、國家安全及敏感個人數據等指定用途，實施獨立安全評估和限期授權要求，並加強模型來源披露。 在半導體領域，委員會提出修改《2018年出口管制改革法》，要求先進AI芯片對華出口商證明，相關交易不會擠佔美國所需的半導體制造及AI產能，涵蓋先進製程晶圓、高帶寬存儲器和先進封裝。 數據安全：提出全國統一授權機制 委員會提出建立“美國數據倡議”，統籌聯邦數據管理及數據資產確認，並建立個人數據主動授權機制。 針對數據經紀商，委員會主張出售或共享個人信息須取得消費者同意，同時禁止向受中國等外國對手司法管轄的人員轉移相關敏感數據，即使消費者同意也不例外。 印太安全：關注臺灣及海底基礎設施 報告將臺灣安全列為重點，認為中國大陸正通過軍事活動、經濟施壓、網絡行動及政治影響等方式改變臺海現狀，並特別關注封鎖、隔離及灰色地帶行動的風險。 委員會還主張美國與盟友加強情報共享、海岸警衛合作及應對經濟脅迫的協調，同時關注臺灣在全球先進半導體供應鏈中的關鍵地位。 在香港方面，報告認為香港正成為中國內地科技企業獲取國際資本、推動人民幣國際化的重要渠道。委員會指出，2026年上半年香港首次公開募股中，內地控股企業按數量計算佔96%，並關注香港金融活動涉及的制裁規避風險，以及國安法律變化對營商環境的影響。

title: 11/20/26 National Security and Korean News and Commentary
zh_title: 26/11/20 国家安全与韩国新闻和评论
source: Small Wars Journal by Arizona State Univ

content:
一年中的大部分时间里，莱特纳平原都没有什么可以为当地人或游客提供的东西。这是布拉格斯巴达足球场对面的一大片毫无特色的土地。表面交替出现灰尘和泥土；有一个巴士停车场，有时还有马戏团。但莱特纳偶尔会举办一些可以让捷克政坛发生倾斜的活动。有时有一点。有时很多。 1989 年 11 月 25 日星期六，大约 75 万人聚集在一起，要求结束捷克斯洛伐克的共产主义政权。第二天，许多人返回，并于 11 月 29 日星期三，议会废除了共产党在社会中的领导地位。这次不会再发生类似的事情，但 11 月 15 日星期日，莱特纳岛上大约有 40 万人参加了自天鹅绒革命以来布拉格最大规模的示威活动。从媒体平台俯瞰旗帜和面孔的海洋时，它看起来很大。数万人聚集在那里抗议政府计划取消每月 10 美元的许可费，该许可费为该国两家公共广播公司捷克电视台和捷克广播电台提供资金。这似乎不是一个令人愤慨的提议，但对许多捷克人来说，这加深了他们对亿万富翁总理安德烈·巴比什及其民粹主义联盟的不信任。这位总理多年来一直在法庭上与欧盟补贴欺诈指控作斗争，他不喜欢公共广播。

For much of the year, Letná Plain has nothing to offer either locals or tourists.  It’s a large, featureless patch of land opposite the Sparta Prague football stadium. The surface alternates between dust and mud; there’s a car park for buses, and sometimes a circus. But every so often, Letná hosts an event that can tilt the world of Czech politics on its axis. Sometimes a little. Sometimes a lot.  On Saturday, November 25, 1989, around 750,000 people gathered to demand the end of Czechoslovakia’s communist regime. The following day, many returned, and on Wednesday, November 29, parliament abolished the Communist Party’s leading role in society. Nothing like that is going to happen this time around, but on Sunday, November 15, there were perhaps 400,000 people on Letná for the largest demonstration in Prague since the Velvet Revolution. It looked huge when viewed from a media platform overlooking an ocean of flags and faces.   The people who had gathered in the tens of thousands were there to protest against government plans to scrap the $10 monthly license fee which funds the nation’s two public broadcasters, Czech TV and Czech Radio. This may not seem an outrageous proposal, but to many Czechs it deepens their distrust of their billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babiš and his populist coalition.   The premier, who has spent years in court fighting EU subsidy fraud allegations , is no fan of public broadcasting.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. In 2017, Babiš, who was then finance minister, described Czech TV’s investigative reporters as “a corrupt rabble making reports to order.” In 2024, he said public broadcasters were part of the then governing coalition’s “media division.”  But it is his coalition ally, the far-right SPD party, that has spearheaded the campaign to scrap the license fees and replace them with direct state funding. The fear is that state funds will come with strings pulled by politicians. Tokyo-born businessman Tomio Okamura, the SPD chairman and now parliament’s speaker, has said he would vote for a bill to abolish the broadcasters altogether if someone submitted one.  The third coalition partner is the MAGA-friendly Motorists for Themselves party, which was against scrapping the fees but is now in favor. One Motorist MP said public broadcasting had been turned into a totem by one half of Czech society, which was giving the other half the finger.  What is clear is that the government has not covered itself in glory. After months of vague and occasionally rancorous debate, and just days after all three coalition parties did poorly in Senate and local elections, the first reading of the bill was rushed through parliament in the middle of the night, with a vote scheduled for 4:36 am on Saturday, October 24. The bill envisages a cut in funding of around 15%, reversing an increase introduced by the previous government. Babiš is also floating alternative funding mechanisms, including voluntary contributions, and insists the government will not interfere in editorial decisions.  But there is a glaring contradiction. His government’s own impact assessment identifies the license fee as the funding mechanism that carries the smallest risk to the broadcasters’ independence. Direct state funding, it says, carries the greatest risk.  There has been much talk of “the Nordic model,” without acknowledging that there is no single Nordic model. Finland and Sweden, for example, have dedicated levies collected through the tax system, but Babiš has ruled out a new tax.  Observers are more worried about “the Slovak model.” There, the license fee was abolished in 2023 with a solemn promise to ringfence funding for Slovak Radio and TV and preserve its independence.  The following year, the broadcaster was dissolved by Robert Fico’s populist nationalist government and replaced. Critics say its successor is now toeing the government line. Babiš said he would not be deterred by mass demonstrations, though there was a tiny wobble from Culture Minister Oto Klempíř, who said after talks with Michael McGrath, the European Commissioner for Democracy and Justice, that he wanted to delay further debate on the bill until parliament had begun discussing legislation to implement the European Media Freedom Act.  The 72-year-old prime minister is in a tough spot. He seems tired and barely invested in the issue while his far-right coalition partner insists the fee has to go. Babiš is known to dislike big demonstrations, and the opposition senses an opportunity.  Following Klempíř’s suggestion to kick the issue into the long grass would be a logical course of action for the prime minister, but it may not be one that’s open to him.  Rob Cameron is a Prague-based journalist and broadcaster, and author of https://www.basedinbohemia.com/ where he writes about Central Europe through reporting, analysis and long-form storytelling.
